preserved_fields.description_medium: During CNN's May 2023 town hall, Trump repeatedly shifted from policy responses to personal attacks toward moderator Kaitlan Collins while the audience reacted in real time. Coverage of the event documented a familiar tactic: discrediting a female journalist through derision and confrontation rather than engagement with the question. The segment became a high-profile example of Trump's televised hostility toward women in journalistic roles.

title: Trump Turned a Supreme Court Hearing Into Another Presidential Power Flex
description_short: Trump Turned a Supreme Court Hearing Into Another Presidential Power Flex
description_medium: PBS described Trump taking a front-row public seat at Supreme Court arguments, something no sitting president had done before, while his administration defended its attack on birthright citizenship. The point was not courtroom etiquette alone. It was the performance of presence, a silent reminder that he treats institutions as stages to loom over, with power performed as proximity, spectacle, and barely disguised pressure.
description_long: Trump sat in the front row of the Supreme Court during oral arguments on April 1, 2026, as the justices considered his administration’s effort to restrict birthright citizenship. PBS described the visit as unprecedented for a sitting president attending arguments in person. The case concerned the administration’s interpretation of citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment and the legal effect of the executive action. Trump’s presence was a public display of presidential attention to a case involving his own policy, but the supplied reporting does not say that he addressed the justices, communicated with them during the hearing, or changed the court’s process. Attendance alone does not establish improper pressure or influence. This entry records the unusual appearance and the case before the Court while separating observable conduct from the source’s interpretation of it as a performance of power. The hearing itself produced no immediate ruling.

title: 2025 reconciliation law requires six-month Medicaid expansion renewals and shortens retroactive coverage
description_short: 2025 reconciliation law requires six-month Medicaid expansion renewals and shortens retroactive coverage
description_medium: The 2025 reconciliation law requires Medicaid expansion adults to renew eligibility every six months rather than annually for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026. Beginning January 1, 2027, it also shortens retroactive coverage to one month before application for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid and CHIP applicants. The law therefore narrows, but does not eliminate, retroactive Medicaid coverage.
description_long: The supplied correction describes two distinct Medicaid changes in the 2025 reconciliation law. For expansion adults, eligibility renewals shift from annual to every six months for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026. Beginning January 1, 2027, retroactive coverage is shortened to one month before application for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid and CHIP applicants. It is not eliminated entirely. More frequent renewals can require enrollees to provide eligibility information sooner, while the shorter look-back period reduces how far back coverage can apply after an application. The specific effects on individual enrollment depend on eligibility and the applicant’s circumstances, which the supplied record does not quantify. This entry uses the corrected dates and periods from KFF and the Congressional Research Service. It replaces the inaccurate claim that retroactive coverage ended completely and distinguishes the renewal requirement from the separate limit on retroactive coverage.

title: Springfield Ohio Disinformation Campaign
description_short: Springfield Ohio Disinformation Campaign
description_medium: Following Trump's debate comments in September 2024, a widespread disinformation campaign targeted Springfield, Ohio, repeating the false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating local pets. The rhetoric led to bomb threats against schools, city buildings, and hospitals, forcing evacuations and closures. Despite the real-world chaos and fear generated in the community, Trump and his allies continued to double down on the baseless claims.
description_long: The Springfield, Ohio, rumor spread after Trump repeated during the September 2024 debate a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets. The accusation circulated widely even though local officials said there was no evidence to support it. Schools, public buildings, and hospitals received bomb threats, leading to evacuations and closures that disrupted community life. The supplied account connects the spread of the rumor with the threats and public-safety response, but does not claim that Trump personally made the threats or identify who sent them. It also does not provide an exact count of threats or a list of each affected institution. This entry records the false allegation, the resulting threats reported in Springfield, and the impact on public services. It treats the claim as disinformation and keeps responsibility for the threats distinct from the people targeted by the rumor.
